title: The new moon
hookLine: O Allah, bring it over us with security and faith (Tirmidhi)
tomorrow: why would anyone pray for the rain to move away?

cards: Sunset, and the family group chat wakes up. Anyone see it? Someone posts a blurry photo: a sliver of light over a parking lot, thin as a thread.

An uncle is up on a roof. A grandmother is squinting from the driveway, pointing with her whole arm. In the Islamic calendar a month begins with the new crescent, so this thin line of light is a door opening.
Now step back into the scene the hadith gives us. The sliver appears, and the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, looks up at it too. He doesn't post anything.
He speaks. And the surprise is who he speaks to.

teach.h: FIRST, TO GOD: SAFETY AND FAITH.
teach.b: He speaks to God first, and then to the moon. The words are kept in the hadith collection of at-Tirmidhi. They begin as a request: O Allah, bring it over us with blessing and faith, with safety and Islam.

teach.h: THEN TO THE MOON: MY LORD AND YOURS.
teach.b: Then he turns to the crescent itself and says: my Lord and your Lord is Allah. Two things are happening in that small prayer.

teach.h: A MONTH GREETED LIKE A GUEST.
teach.b: First, the month is greeted like a guest who could be carrying anything. Nobody knows yet what's inside it: an exam, a wedding, a hard diagnosis, a raise. So the first ask isn't for success.
It's for safety and faith: that whatever this month holds, it arrives in peace and finds you still holding on. Second, the moon is put in its place, gently.
The Qur'an tells of Ibrahim watching a moon rise and set, and saying, in Pickthall's words, "I love not things that set." This prayer does the same work in one friendly sentence.
The crescent is beautiful, and it is a creature like us, answering to the same Lord. Nobody is asked to worship the light, or to fear it. And notice the shape this gives a year.
A calendar can feel like a conveyor belt.
Here, every month opens with a door, a sky worth looking up at, and the same short words.

how: Many Muslims look for the new crescent at sunset at the start of a month and say the Prophet's words from at-Tirmidhi's collection, asking for blessing, faith, safety and Islam, and ending: my Lord and your Lord is Allah.

o: the thin crescent whose sighting opens each Islamic month
an eclipse that calls Muslims to a special prayer
the full moon that marks the middle of a fasting month

games.q: what's in the prayer — tap the pairs.
p: I love not things that set

s: the prayer at the new moon is said to the moon, asking it for luck
it asks God for blessing and faith, then tells the moon: my Lord and your Lord is Allah.
in the Islamic calendar, a month begins with the new crescent
that's why families look for that thin line of light at sunset.
the prayer asks first for a successful month
it asks for blessing and faith, safety and Islam: peace first, whatever the month holds.

games.q: your cousin starts a new job on the first of the month and texts: 'pray i crush it.' you know the new-moon words. what fits them best?
o: may this month come to you in safety and faith, whatever it holds.
may this month bring you the success you've been working for.
may the new moon bring you good luck on day one.
games.why: the Prophet's words at the crescent ask for blessing and faith, safety and Islam. success isn't refused; it just isn't the first ask.

practice: Take a pen and write the name of the month you're in at the top of a page. Under it, write one thing you already know this month holds, and one you can't know yet. For the sit, rest your eyes on that second line.

wordCard.voice: The new moon. The thin crescent that opens each month in the Islamic calendar, greeted with a request for safety and faith, and a reminder: my Lord and your Lord is Allah.

orig.note: Arabic: hilal, the new crescent moon that opens the month.

carryVoice: Carry this: a new month, in peace. The sky is worth a look at sunset.
